topic: Responsive layout patterns for data-dense operational web apps (ERIS: Caltrans geotechnical emergency response) across phone 360-430px, tablet/iPad 768-1024px portrait and landscape, and desktop: tables to cards, master-detail to drill-in, side rails to bottom navigation, progressive disclosure, density modes, touch targets

findings.principle: Material 3 window size classes are the most device-representative breakpoint set: compact < 600dp (99.96% of phones in portrait), medium 600-839dp (93.73% of tablets in portrait), expanded 840-1199dp (97.22% of tablets in landscape), large 1200-1599dp, extra-large >= 1600dp (desktops). Height classes also matter: compact height < 480dp covers 99.78% of phones in landscape.
findings.applicability: ERIS should adopt four width tokens (600 / 840 / 1200 CSS px) rather than device names. iPad portrait (768-834 CSS px on 9.7-11 inch models) falls in medium, so it must work as a single-pane, drill-in layout; iPad landscape (1024-1194 px) and the 12.9 inch iPad in portrait (1024 px) fall in expanded and get two panes; desktops >= 1200 px get three regions (nav + list + detail, or form + supporting pane). Treat a phone in landscape (compact height) as a case where sticky headers and bottom bars must shrink.

findings.principle: The list-detail canonical layout shows list and detail side by side only in expanded width; in medium and compact width it shows either the list or the detail, selecting an item replaces the list with the detail, and Back redisplays the list. When the window shrinks from expanded to medium/compact the detail pane stays visible (not the list); when it grows, list plus selected detail (or a placeholder) appear together.
findings.applicability: This is the model for the maintenance coordinator's incident triage queue, the branch chief's routing queue, and the reviewer's approval queue. On desktop and iPad landscape: queue on the left (about 1/3 to 40%) and the selected incident/assessment on the right. On iPad portrait and phones: the same routes become a drill-in stack with a Back affordance, and rotating the iPad must not lose the open incident (preserve selection state in the URL, e.g. /incidents/123, so it survives resize and reload).

findings.principle: The supporting pane canonical layout splits primary (about 2/3) and secondary (about 1/3) content in expanded width, splits them equally in medium width, and in compact width moves the secondary content into a bottom sheet, side sheet, or below the primary content reachable via a button. Esri Calcite adds that its Shell does not auto-hide slotted panels on small screens; developers should programmatically set collapsed on a Shell Panel under a viewport width and consider moving a Panel from panel-start/panel-end to panel-bottom to fit the thumb zone of a phone.
findings.applicability: The GISA technical form is primary content; the site map, cross-section, and photo gallery are supporting content that only make sense next to the form. On desktop keep them in a right-hand pane (about 1/3), on iPad landscape 50/50 or collapsible, on iPad portrait and phones present them as a bottom sheet opened from a sticky 'Map / Photos' button. Do not rely on the map library to collapse itself; wire the collapse to the ERIS breakpoint tokens.

findings.principle: Material's adaptive navigation rule: use a bottom navigation bar when width or height is compact, and a navigation rail otherwise; optionally a navigation drawer at expanded width or above. The stated reason is reachability: on a phone the bottom bar is within thumb reach, while on a tablet held by its left and right edges a rail alongside the content is easier to reach.
findings.applicability: ERIS role navigation (Incidents, Assessments, Map, Approvals/Tasks, Admin) should render as a bottom bar under 600 px, a 72-80 px icon rail from 600 px (iPad portrait), and an expanded rail or persistent sidebar with labels at >= 1200 px. Keep the destination set identical across sizes so a coordinator who triages on an iPad in the field and finishes on a desktop sees the same structure.

findings.principle: Apple HIG Layout: iPad windows are fluidly resizable (Split View, Slide Over, Stage Manager), so designers must account for the full range of sizes, design the full-screen layout first and 'defer switching to a compact view for as long as possible', and test at the system-provided halves, thirds, and quadrants on a variety of devices. Layout guides should restrict text width for readability and respect safe areas.
findings.applicability: Field staff will run ERIS beside Photos, Files, or Maps in Split View, producing widths around 507 px (1/3), 678 px (1/2 on 12.9 inch), and 834 px (2/3). ERIS must therefore be fluid between breakpoints, not designed only at 768 and 1024. Use container-relative widths and CSS container queries for the queue/detail regions so a half-width ERIS window degrades to medium or compact behaviour gracefully rather than snapping early.

findings.principle: Apple HIG on iPad panes and tabs: a split view can have two or three vertical panes; designers must 'account for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths' and 'persistently highlight the current selection in each pane'. On iPadOS the tab bar appears near the top and can convert to a sidebar; aim for a default of five or fewer tabs to preserve continuity between compact and regular sizes; use a tab bar for navigation, not for actions.
findings.applicability: Cap ERIS top-level destinations at five per role (put Admin/Users and Settings behind a 'More' or profile menu for non-admins). In the two-pane queue view, keep the selected incident row visibly highlighted while its detail is open. Never place actions such as 'Assign', 'Approve', or 'Submit GISA' in the navigation bar or bottom nav; those belong in a toolbar or a sticky action bar within the content.

findings.principle: Touch target sizing converges across sources: Apple lists a 44x44 pt default and 28x28 pt minimum control size for iOS/iPadOS with about 12 pt padding around bezeled elements and about 24 pt around bezel-less ones; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires 24x24 CSS px unless a 24 px circle centered on each target does not intersect another target, with an 'essential' exception for things like digital maps; NN/g recommends a physical 1 cm x 1 cm target with about 2 mm spacing, based on Parhi, Karlson and Bederson (2006).
findings.applicability: ERIS policy: every interactive element >= 24x24 CSS px everywhere (AA floor), and >= 44x44 px on coarse pointers (iPad, phone) via an @media (pointer: coarse) rule that enlarges row-action icons, table sort headers, chips, and checkbox hit areas. Row height on touch devices should be >= 48 px. Map pins/vertices on the site map can rely on the WCAG 'essential' exception, but the map's own toolbar buttons cannot.

findings.principle: USWDS provides two accessible mobile table transformations, usa-table--stacked and usa-table--stacked-header, which collapse rows to a single column and render each cell's data-label attribute as an inline label via ::before; the SCSS applies them with at-media-max('mobile-lg'), i.e. below the 480 px mobile-lg breakpoint. Wide tables otherwise use usa-table-container--scrollable and usa-table--sticky-header, and every table needs a caption and scope on headers; sortable headers need aria-sort.
findings.applicability: For the admin Users table and any secondary tables (attachments, history) ERIS can use the stacked-header approach on phones: keep the semantic <table>, add data-label to every cell, and stack under 480 px. For the primary incident/assessment queues a purpose-built card list is better (see patterns), but the stacked table is the low-cost fallback that keeps sorting and screen-reader semantics intact.

findings.principle: GOV.UK Design System table guidance: use tables to compare and scan, never for layout; 'aim to have less data in your tables' and split large datasets into multiple tables or pages; right-align numeric columns with the --numeric modifiers; the govuk-table--small-text-until-tablet class is only for tables with a lot of data because 'a smaller amount of data is easier to read if the text is larger'. GOV.UK breakpoints are mobile 320 px, tablet 641 px, desktop 769 px with a default 1020 px maximum page width.
findings.applicability: Limit the ERIS incident queue to 6-7 columns at desktop (ID, route/postmile, type, priority, status, reported, assignee) and move everything else into the detail pane. Right-align numeric columns such as postmile, elevation, and slope angle. Do not shrink text below 16 px on iPad to squeeze extra columns; instead hide low-priority columns and expose them via a column picker.

findings.principle: GOV.UK 'one thing per page' and the service manual: starting with one question per page helps users understand what is asked, focus, find their way through an unfamiliar process, 'use the service on a mobile device', and recover from errors, and lets the service save answers automatically, capture per-question analytics, and handle branching. Grouping related questions on one page is acceptable, especially for internal services where staff switch tasks quickly, guided by user research. Use a summary list (key-value rows with 'Change' links and pre-populated answers) for the check-answers step. NN/g adds that progressive disclosure should stay within two levels; beyond that users get lost.
findings.applicability: Structure the GISA form as named sections (Site, Geology, Hazard, Recommendations, Photos, Attachments) with autosave per field. On compact widths render one section per screen with a stepper; on expanded widths show sections stacked with a sticky section table of contents. Finish with a summary-list 'Review your GISA' page that reviewers also see. Keep disclosure to two levels: section -> optional 'Advanced parameters' expander, never nested expanders inside expanders.

findings.principle: IBM Carbon data table defines five row sizes: extra small 24 px, small 32 px, medium 40 px, large 48 px, extra large 64 px (xl only when rows have two lines of content), with the header row matching the row size. Selecting rows surfaces a batch action bar at the top of the table; the toolbar is reserved for global actions with up to five visible; expandable rows hold supplementary data and should move to a dedicated page if cramped.
findings.applicability: Give ERIS queues a density control with three of Carbon's sizes: compact 32 px, default 40 px, comfortable 48 px. Default to 48 px on coarse pointers and 40 px on desktops, persist the choice per user, and never offer 24 px. Use a Carbon-style batch bar for 'Assign to engineer' and 'Route to branch' on multi-select, limit the toolbar to five actions (search, filter, sort, columns, export), and use expandable rows only for short supplementary facts such as last update or location notes.

findings.principle: Enterprise design systems converge on similar breakpoints but key them to the viewport: Carbon sm 320 / md 672 / lg 1056 / xlg 1312 / max 1584 px with 4, 8, 16 columns; Atlassian xxs 320-479, xs 480-767, s 768-1023, m 1024-1439, l 1440-1767, xl 1768+ and states that 'breakpoints are based on the viewport width, not the width of the main content area', advising designers to cover at least two sizes and always include mobile; Polaris tokens are xs 0 / sm 490 / md 768 / lg 1040 / xl 1440 px; Fluent 2 uses small 320-479, medium 480-639, large 640-1023, x-large 1024-1365, xx-large 1366-1919, xxx-large 1920+ and names five adaptation techniques: reposition, resize, reflow, show/hide, re-architect; USWDS uses mobile 320, mobile-lg 480, tablet 640, tablet-lg 880, desktop 1024, desktop-lg 1200, widescreen 1400 with min-width (mobile-first) queries.
findings.applicability: ERIS should publish a small, documented token set: 480 (stack tables), 600 (compact/medium), 840 (two panes), 1200 (three regions / full table), 1440 (max content width, cap dense pages so 27 inch monitors do not produce 200-character rows). Write mobile-first min-width media queries for page chrome and container queries for the queue/detail regions, and decide layout per Fluent's ladder (reflow first, show/hide second, re-architect only at the 600 and 840 boundaries).

findings.principle: NN/g research on mobile tables: build a usable desktop table first and then adapt it; keep column headers sticky and lock the first column during horizontal scroll so context is retained; let users choose which columns/rows to see (before viewing when comparison is not needed, during viewing when it is); group related data into accordions; signal horizontal overflow with visibly cut-off columns or arrows rather than dots; keep columns legible without zoom; and do not treat device rotation as the solution because it sacrifices rows. Polaris IndexTable applies the same ideas: sticky header and sticky last column, pagination above 50 items, rows that navigate to the resource detail, and a condensed mode below 490 px that hides bulk actions (so only use it when bulk actions are not essential).
findings.applicability: At 840-1199 px (iPad landscape) keep the incident queue as a real table with sticky header, sticky ID/route column, horizontally scrollable secondary columns with a visible cut-off, and a column picker. Below 840 px switch to condensed rows (Polaris style): route/postmile as the title, priority and status chips, reported time, assignee avatar, chevron to detail. Paginate or virtualize past 50 rows. Because condensed mode drops bulk selection, ensure every batch action also exists as a per-row action in the detail view.

findings.principle: NN/g's hidden-navigation study: hiding navigation behind a hamburger reduced content discoverability by more than 20% on both desktop and mobile; desktop tasks were 39% slower and mobile tasks 15% slower than with visible or combo navigation; users rated hidden navigation 21% harder. Recommendation: do not use hidden navigation on desktop, and on mobile show up to four top-level links visibly, hiding the rest only when space runs out; 'mobile-first' must not become 'mobile-only' on desktop.
findings.applicability: ERIS must not collapse role navigation into a hamburger on desktops or iPads in landscape; the rail or sidebar stays visible. On phones the bottom bar carries the four most-used destinations for the role (e.g. coordinator: Incidents, Map, Tasks, Profile) with the rest under a fifth 'More' item. Combine icon and label on the rail for rotating public-sector staff who may not have memorised icons.

findings.principle: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.10 Reflow (Level AA) requires content to present without two-dimensional scrolling at 320 CSS px width (equivalent to 1280 px at 400% zoom). Content that requires two-dimensional layout is exempt, explicitly including data tables and maps and interfaces where toolbars must stay in view, but the exemption does not extend to individual table cells or to surrounding headings, search fields, and form controls, which must still reflow.
findings.applicability: A wide incident table and the site map may scroll horizontally on a phone (or at 400% zoom on a desktop, which Caltrans accessibility reviews will test), but the page header, filters, search, GISA form fields, and dialog contents must never require horizontal scrolling at 320 px. Test every ERIS page at 1280 px wide with 400% browser zoom, not only on a phone emulator.

patterns.pattern: Window-size-class tokens (compact / medium / expanded / large) driven by viewport width, with container queries inside the content region
patterns.whenToUse: Everywhere; define once in the design system so every screen adapts on the same boundaries and iPad Split View or Stage Manager widths are handled fluidly instead of by device detection.
patterns.erisApplication: Tokens: compact < 600 px (phones, 1/3-width iPad Split View), medium 600-839 px (iPad portrait, 1/2-width Split View on 12.9 inch), expanded 840-1199 px (iPad landscape, small laptops), large >= 1200 px (desktops), plus a 480 px stacking threshold for tables and a 1440 px max content width. Expose them as CSS custom properties and a useWindowSizeClass hook; no user-agent sniffing for 'iPad'.

patterns.pattern: List-detail that becomes a drill-in stack (Material canonical list-detail / Apple split view)
patterns.whenToUse: Queues where each item has an independently meaningful detail: incident triage, assessment routing, review/approval, user management.
patterns.erisApplication: Expanded and large: queue pane 360-480 px wide on the left with sticky filters, detail on the right, selected row persistently highlighted, URL carries the selected ID. Medium and compact: queue fills the width, tapping a row pushes the detail full-screen with a Back control and the queue's scroll position preserved; shrinking the window while a detail is open keeps the detail visible. Provide next/previous within the detail so a coordinator can triage sequentially without returning to the list on an iPad in portrait.

patterns.pattern: Responsive table ladder: full table -> prioritised columns with sticky header and first column -> condensed rows/cards (with a USWDS stacked-header fallback for secondary tables)
patterns.whenToUse: Any collection with more than four attributes where users compare and sort on desktop but scan and act on mobile.
patterns.erisApplication: >= 1200 px: full incident table (6-7 columns, density toggle, batch bar). 840-1199 px: same table with column priorities (always: ID/route, priority, status; hide first: reporter, last updated) hidden columns available via a column picker, sticky header and ID column, visibly cut-off horizontal overflow. < 840 px: condensed row cards with title, two chips, one timestamp, one avatar, chevron; sort and filter move to a bottom sheet; pagination or virtualization above 50 rows. Admin Users and attachment tables use USWDS-style data-label stacking below 480 px so they stay semantic tables.

patterns.pattern: Adaptive role navigation: bottom bar (compact) -> icon rail (medium/expanded) -> labelled rail or sidebar (large), never a hamburger-only menu on desktop
patterns.whenToUse: Apps with 3-5 top-level destinations used by staff across phones, iPads and desktops who need the same mental model on every device.
patterns.erisApplication: Per-role destination sets capped at five: Coordinator (Incidents, Map, Tasks, Notifications, More), Chief (Queue, Assessments, Map, Reports, More), Engineer (My assessments, GISA drafts, Map, Photos, More), Reviewer (Approvals, Assessments, Map, More), Admin adds Users under More or a dedicated rail item. Bottom bar under 600 px with labels always shown; 80 px rail from 600 px; rail expands to a 240 px sidebar with labels at >= 1200 px. Actions (Assign, Approve, Submit) never live in navigation.

patterns.pattern: Long-form progressive disclosure: sections as steps on compact, stacked sections with sticky table of contents on expanded, supporting pane for map and photos, summary-list review before submit, autosave throughout
patterns.whenToUse: Forms longer than one screen that are filled over multiple sessions or in the field, with reference material (maps, photos) that must be consulted while typing.
patterns.erisApplication: GISA form: six named sections with completion state. Compact: one section per screen, stepper at top, sticky bottom bar with Back / Save / Next, map and photos via a bottom sheet. Expanded: single-column fields (max 640 px measure) with a sticky section TOC on the left and the map/photo supporting pane on the right (about 1/3), collapsible on iPad landscape. Advanced parameters live one level deep in an expander; nothing deeper. 'Review your GISA' uses a summary list with Change links that return to a pre-populated section; the same view serves reviewers.

patterns.pattern: Density modes tied to pointer type: compact 32 px / default 40 px / comfortable 48 px rows
patterns.whenToUse: Data tables and lists where desktop power users want to see more rows but touch users need larger targets.
patterns.erisApplication: Density toggle in the table toolbar (one of the five allowed toolbar actions), stored per user. Default: 48 px when @media (pointer: coarse) matches (iPad, phone), 40 px on fine pointers; 32 px available only on fine pointers. Density changes row height, cell padding and chip size, but form controls keep their 44 px touch height regardless. Header row always matches the row size.

patterns.pattern: Touch-target policy with a coarse-pointer override
patterns.whenToUse: Any control that appears on both desktop and iPad/phone.
patterns.erisApplication: Global floor 24x24 CSS px with 8 px spacing (WCAG 2.5.8). Under @media (pointer: coarse): 44x44 px minimum for buttons, row action icons, sort headers, chips, checkboxes (hit area enlarged with padding, not necessarily the visible glyph), map toolbar buttons, and 48 px list rows. Map pins and cross-section handles may be smaller under the 'essential' exception but must have a list-based alternative (select the incident from the queue).

patterns.pattern: Supporting pane -> bottom sheet for map, cross-section and photos (Calcite-informed)
patterns.whenToUse: Secondary content that is only meaningful alongside primary content and is map- or image-heavy.
patterns.erisApplication: >= 1200 px: right-hand pane about 1/3 width, resizable, with map, cross-section and photo tabs. 840-1199 px: pane collapsible to a 48 px edge strip; default collapsed on iPad landscape when the GISA form is being edited. < 840 px: floating 'Map' and 'Photos' buttons open a half-height bottom sheet that can expand to full screen; collapse state is driven by ERIS breakpoints, not by the map component. Map interactions are exempt from reflow but the sheet header and controls reflow at 320 px.

patterns.pattern: Batch actions on selection with per-item fallback on phones, and a sticky action bar for form submission
patterns.whenToUse: Queues where chiefs or coordinators assign or route many items at once on desktop, but phone users act on one item at a time.
patterns.erisApplication: Desktop and iPad: selecting rows replaces the toolbar with a batch bar (Assign, Route, Set priority, Export) and disables per-row overflow menus while active. Under 490-600 px: multi-select is hidden and each condensed row keeps a swipe or overflow action plus the same actions in the detail view. GISA form and review screens have a sticky bottom action bar (Save draft / Submit / Approve / Return) that stays above the iPad keyboard and the phone bottom navigation.

antiPatterns: Hiding role navigation behind a hamburger on desktop or iPad landscape; NN/g measured more than 20% lower discoverability and 39% slower desktop tasks with hidden navigation.

Squeezing the full desktop incident table onto a phone by shrinking text or forcing two-dimensional scrolling of cells; WCAG reflow exempts whole tables and maps but not cells, headings, filters or form fields at 320 px.
Treating device rotation as the mobile table strategy; NN/g notes it sacrifices rows and users rarely do it, so provide column priorities or condensed rows instead.

Keying breakpoints to device names or user-agent strings ('iPad', 'iPhone') or to the content-area width; breakpoints must be viewport-based so Split View, Stage Manager and side panels behave predictably (Atlassian, Apple).
Switching to the compact layout as soon as the iPad leaves full screen; Apple advises deferring the compact view for as long as the full layout still fits.
Placing actions (Assign, Approve, Submit) in the bottom navigation or tab bar; tab bars are for navigation, actions belong in toolbars or sticky action bars (Apple HIG).
Offering more than five top-level destinations, or a different set per device, breaking continuity between compact and regular sizes (Apple, NN/g).
Using the 24 px or 32 px compact row density on touch devices, or any target under 24x24 CSS px anywhere; iPad controls should default to 44x44 pt and rows to 48 px.
Nesting progressive disclosure more than two levels deep in the GISA form (section -> expander -> expander); NN/g finds users get lost beyond two levels.
Hiding bulk actions in condensed mode without giving every batch action a per-item equivalent, or hiding priority/status columns in condensed rows with no way to reveal them.
Building one long single-page GISA form on phones with no autosave, no section steps and no review step; GOV.UK's one-thing-per-page research shows this hurts mobile use and error recovery.
Letting the map or photo component decide its own collapse behaviour (Calcite Shell does not auto-hide panels); collapse must be driven by the app's breakpoint tokens.
Using tables for page layout or for key-value detail views; use the grid for layout and a summary list for incident/assessment facts (GOV.UK).

Designing the phone layout first and stretching it to desktop ('mobile-only'), producing single-column desktop queues with 200-character rows; design the desktop table first, cap content width around 1440 px, then adapt down (NN/g).
